On ESG. The obvious problem with ESG was that it was being driven by marketing rather than outcomes. If the focus was only on the E - ESG investing might have made sense. Even here it is tricky. For several years the biggest shift away from carbon in the U.S. was from switching coal to natural gas power. Does that mean that ESG funds should be buying natural gas pipeline companies? But the S & the G not only have different definitions they frequently have contradictory criteria. Is it a good social policy to be pro-life or pro-abortion? To favor transgenderism or to treat it as something that is dangerous for young people? The answers are very much in the eyes of the beholder. Something similar can be said about governance. As someone who has been investing for more than 40 years, I prefer board members who have very large equity ownership in the company. Most governance standards value indepence. On balance, it is a great outcome that ESG has largely faded into the background.

Surprised that he's invested in his employer. It's common advice - which I support - that doing that is placing too many eggs in one basket. You're already heavily invested in your employer by being dependent on the company's continuing success for your income. If the company hits hard times you've got increased odds of being out of a job. And if you're also invested in them, you're both out of a job/no income, AND your savings are being devalued as well at the same time that you're personally having hard times because you've lost employment income. 

If you receive stock as part of your employment income, you should move that out of being invested in your employer when you are able.

Edit: not that Ben recommended doing this - he didn't - nor did he say that his holding is a substantial amount of his savings are in it. That would be bad. A token amount would be fine.

Man, as a software engineer, all these finance bros talking about bitcoin makes me die a little inside. I had huge respect for Ben Felix, which he lost quite a bit here.

Bitcoin did not solve any problems that wasn't solved before. Period.
What bitcoin does is defining a way to reach a consensus. In bitcoin's case, it is based on majority of computing power. That is literally it. Nothing else, no magic, no defi bs.

Imagine you have a group of people using bitcoin. There is a transaction that 51% recognizes while 49% does not. In terms of bitcoin's logic, the group must follow the 51%.
But there  is LITERALLY NOTHING stopping 49% simply not recognizing it. They can literally walk away and say their version where transaction did not happen is the correct version.

This is literally how a "consensus" works. If a collective agrees on something, it is agreed. If they do not, it is not. And sky is blue.
Bitcoin did not solve shit. It only defined a method and in no way better than other methods unless you value wasting energy to determine who in fact has the biggest computing power.

For several years the biggest shift away from carbon in the U.S. was from switching coal to natural gas power. Does that mean that ESG funds should be buying natural gas pipeline companies? But the S & the G not only have different definitions they frequently have contradictory criteria. Is it a good social policy to be pro-life or pro-abortion? To favor transgenderism or to treat it as something that is dangerous for young people? The answers are very much in the eyes of the beholder. Something similar can be said about governance. As someone who has been investing for more than 40 years, I prefer board members who have very large equity ownership in the company. Most governance standards value indepence. On balance, it is a great outcome that ESG has largely faded into the background.

Surprised that he's invested in his employer. It's common advice - which I support - that doing that is placing too many eggs in one basket. You're already heavily invested in your employer by being dependent on the company's continuing success for your income. If the company hits hard times you've got increased odds of being out of a job. And if you're also invested in them, you're both out of a job/no income, AND your savings are being devalued as well at the same time that you're personally having hard times because you've lost employment income. 

If you receive stock as part of your employment income, you should move that out of being invested in your employer when you are able.

Edit: not that Ben recommended doing this - he didn't - nor did he say that his holding is a substantial amount of his savings are in it. That would be bad. A token amount would be fine.

I’ve found Ben’s work and the Rational Reminder content valuable, particularly the emphasis on evidence, costs, transparency, and critically evaluating the financial industry. That’s why my recent experience with PWL’s intake process was disappointing.

Early in the call, I directly asked about fees. Rather than answering at that point, I was told we would get to them later, and the intake questions continued. When we eventually discussed pricing, I learned that the advisory fee at lower asset levels can be around 1.25%. Had I known that beforehand, I likely would not have scheduled the call.

I understand that PWL appears to offer comprehensive financial planning rather than simply portfolio management, and there may be clients for whom the service fully justifies the cost. My concern is less about whether PWL is entitled to charge that fee and more about transparency around it. I was told that PWL does not publish its fee schedule because of compliance requirements and regulatory considerations, but from a prospective client’s perspective, the experience felt much more like a sales process than the transparent, evidence-driven approach I had expected from the educational content associated with the firm.

For a comprehensive planning relationship, trust and transparency are especially important. I would have preferred to see the approximate fee schedule disclosed upfront—or at minimum to receive a direct answer when I explicitly asked about it. For me, there was a significant disconnect between the principles I associate with the educational content and the client experience I encountered.

Just my two cents, you can take it or leave it.

@BenFelixCSI Thank you for acknowledging the comment.

The expectations I’ve formed around the services PWL offers have, in large part, been informed by your educational content. That is why my experience with the firm was disappointing: the service I encountered did not meet the expectations that your work had helped establish.

I recognize that those expectations are ultimately my own. Ideals and values are aspirational, and organizations, like individuals, will inevitably fall short of them at times. Could I simply adjust my expectations? Of course.

That said, your recent Rational Reminder discussion of the halo effect—particularly as it applies to financial influencers—offers an interesting lens through which to evaluate your own work and its relationship with PWL.

There is Ben Felix as an individual producing educational content on YouTube and elsewhere, and there is Ben Felix as a partner at PWL, producing content associated with the firm, including Rational Reminder, while also helping guide the business within the scope of your role. PWL itself has publicly acknowledged that this approach to education and content has been beneficial to the business.

Your work sets a very high bar for quality. I also think it encourages others to improve the quality and rigour of their own work. Inevitably, though, that creates a halo around the organization with which your name and work are closely associated.

An intake call is a crucial initial point of contact with that organization. I think it is reasonable to expect that experience to reflect the same qualities—rigour, transparency, efficiency and thoughtfulness—that characterize the educational content associated with PWL.

For those of us who have followed your work for nearly a decade, there is an additional irony here: you have essentially taught us to approach financial decisions systematically, to be conscious of behavioural biases, to examine incentives and processes, and to favour evidence over impressions. Naturally, some of us are going to apply that same framework when evaluating PWL.

Having to arrange an intake call, have it run beyond the allotted 15 minutes, spend more time than expected going through the process, and only then gain access to the firm’s fee schedule, after asking for it directly closer to the start of the call, does not strike me as particularly transparent. More importantly, it feels inconsistent with the standard of transparency that PWL’s public-facing educational content appears to represent.

This is simply my perspective, and I recognize that PWL is doing well without my two cents and will almost certainly continue to do so.

And I think there is a legitimate point worth considering: when I click on a Ben Felix video, I am watching Ben Felix. It is your name, reputation and credibility that I initially encounter—not PWL’s.

That credibility inevitably creates expectations of the firm behind you. If the halo effect is worth examining when it benefits other financial firms and influencers, I think it is equally worth examining when it benefits PWL.

Lastly, I hope none of this comes across as unnecessarily harsh or rude. My intention is simply to offer feedback from the perspective of someone who has followed your work for a long time. I’m genuinely grateful for the work you do. I perceive much of your educational work as a public service, and it has been extremely helpful to me and, I’m sure, many others. I wish you and your family continued health, happiness and success, and thank you again for everything you’ve contributed.
